# File type filtering

All of ripgrep's file type machinery lives in two modules of the `ignore` crate:
`ignore::types` (public, `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`) and
`ignore::default_types` (crate-private, `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`).
Everything else, including the `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`,
`--type-clear` and `--type-list` flags, is a thin caller.

## How a definition is represented

A definition is a `FileTypeDef`: a `name: String` and a `globs: Vec<String>`.
Both fields are private, exposed through `name()` and `globs()`. There is no
notion of an extension, a MIME type or a language. A type is a name plus a list
of glob strings, and nothing more.

The defaults are a static table, `DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])]`. Each
entry pairs a list of *names* with a list of *globs*, so aliases are expressed
by giving several names to one glob list: `(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])`
becomes two independent `FileTypeDef` values with identical globs. Nothing links
them afterwards, so clearing `bat` leaves `batch` intact.

`TypesBuilder` holds definitions in a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` keyed by
name, plus an ordered `Vec<Selection<()>>` of the selections you've made.
`Selection` is a two-variant enum, `Select(String, T)` and `Negate(String, T)`,
generic over a payload that's `()` while building and `FileTypeDef` after
resolution.

Four builder entry points mutate definitions. `add(name, glob)` appends one glob
to a type, creating it if needed, and rejects the name `all` along with any name
containing a character that isn't `char::is_alphanumeric`. `add_def(def)` parses
the string form users type: `{name}:{glob}` routes to `add`, while
`{name}:include:{a,b,c}` copies the globs of already-defined types into the new
one. The include branch checks that every referenced type exists *before*
copying anything, so a bad include leaves the builder untouched. That atomicity
is asserted by `types::tests::test_invalid_defs`. `clear(name)` removes a
definition outright, and `add_defaults()` walks `DEFAULT_TYPES`.

`select(name)` and `negate(name)` push onto the selection vector. Both treat
`all` specially by expanding it over `self.types.keys()`, which is `HashMap`
iteration order, so the relative order of the expanded selections isn't
deterministic. That doesn't change the verdict when every expansion has the same
polarity, but it does affect which `FileTypeDef` gets reported as responsible.

## How the matcher is built

`TypesBuilder::build()` resolves selections against definitions and returns
`Types`. For each selection it looks up the named definition, returning
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType` if it's missing, clones it into the selection's
payload, then adds every one of its globs to a `globset::GlobSetBuilder` with
`literal_separator(true)`. Alongside, it pushes `(isel, iglob)` onto
`glob_to_selection`, so glob sequence numbers in the finished `GlobSet` map back
to the selection that contributed them. Glob compilation failures become
`Error::Glob`.

`build()` also precomputes `has_selected`: true when at least one selection is a
`Select`. This is the flag that turns "didn't match" into "ignore", and it's the
mechanism behind the rule that selecting any type excludes everything else.

The resulting `Types` carries the sorted, complete `defs` list (used by
`--type-list`), the resolved `selections`, `has_selected`, `glob_to_selection`,
the `GlobSet`, and `matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` from `regex_automata`. The
pool hands each walker thread a scratch vector so matching a path allocates
nothing. `Types` is `Clone` and is stored as `Arc<Types>` in
`ignore::dir::IgnoreOptions`.

## How matching works

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns `Match<Glob<'a>>`. It bails out with
`Match::None` for directories and for an empty glob set, so type filters never
prune traversal. It then reduces the path to its final component with
`pathutil::file_name` and matches against that alone. Every default glob is a
basename glob for this reason; a glob containing `/` in `DEFAULT_TYPES` could
never match.

`GlobSet::matches_into` fills the pooled vector with matching sequence numbers in
ascending order, and `matched` takes `matches.last()`. Because globs entered the
set in selection order, the last match belongs to the latest selection, so the
last flag on the command line wins: `-tmd -Txx` lists nothing while `-Txx -tmd`
lists your Markdown. A winning `Select` yields `Match::Whitelist`, a `Negate`
yields `Match::Ignore`, and both carry a `Glob` borrowing the responsible
`FileTypeDef`. With no match, `has_selected` decides between
`Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` and `Match::None`.

`Ignore::matched` in `dir.rs` consults types after overrides and after the
gitignore stack, and skips them when `Types::is_empty()` reports zero
selections. In
`walk.rs`, `should_skip_entry` acts on the result, but `Walk::skip_entry` returns
early for `depth() == 0`, so an explicitly named file argument is searched
regardless of its type.

## Notes for contributors

Adding a default type means one tuple in `DEFAULT_TYPES`, kept sorted by first
name (`default_types_are_sorted` enforces it) and wrapped to 79 columns. Prefer
basename globs. On the CLI side, `flags::hiargs::types` replays
`LowArgs::type_changes` onto a builder seeded with `add_defaults()`, so ordering
between `--type-clear` and `--type-add` is exactly the order the flags appeared.

Two details tend to surprise. The `iglob` half of `glob_to_selection` is
recorded but never read by `matched`; it exists for finer-grained reporting that
doesn't happen yet. And `TypesBuilder::definitions()` sorts each definition's
globs on its clone, while `build()` clones the unsorted originals into
selections, so `Glob::file_type_def().globs()` returns insertion order while
`--type-list` prints sorted order.
